got_right: Information type is randomized and registered: misinformation -18.2 points (CI [-20.4,-16.0]) and fact-check -13.3 points, with the plausibility replication (-18.6, -12.4) agreeing. The result is robust to dropping trial 1 (-0.170).
Anchoring headlines to real contacts named by respondents gives an ecologically realistic ego-network stimulus, and the report openly labels the sharer traits as measured rather than randomized.
Re-weighting and drop-trial sensitivity checks were reported, and the report discloses its uncorrected test count (about 14 registered tests plus about 180 subgroup contrasts).
The topic split (E2) surfaced a useful heterogeneity: the fact-check effect is -0.151 for political items but -0.028 (SE 0.028) for health items.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Trust and tie strength, the substantive sharer findings, are respondent ratings of real contacts, so they are confounded with unmeasured contact traits. Only information type was randomized.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: H5 high trust +5.7 points and H2 close tie +3.0 points are labelled 'measured contrast'. U1 is unresolved.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: The low-trust reference cell is thin, so the trust contrasts are imprecise and the MDE exceeds the mid-trust estimate. The null results are uninformative for effects below roughly 3 points.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Trust: low n=828, MDE 0.051 to 0.056, against mid-trust estimate 0.036 (p=0.056). MDEs for H3, H4 and H7 are 0.029 to 0.032, and these MDEs ignore clustering.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: A paired forced choice mechanically links misinformation and true-content sharing, so the belief-in-disputed-claims result cannot show an absolute increase. There is no opt-out and no behavioural sharing outcome.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: S3: misinformation +5.6 points and true/neutral -5.5 points (mirrored). U2 is unresolved.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Health items are few and topic was not randomized, so the pooled fact-check claim hides a topic difference.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: E2: Health n=1,110, fact-check -0.028 (SE 0.028) versus Political -0.151; pooled -0.133. U3 is unresolved.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Many uncorrected subgroup contrasts and fragile single-test findings leave the heterogeneity results tentative.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: About 180 uncorrected contrasts; H4 moderate sharer p=0.034 becomes p=0.056 re-weighted; standard errors clustered by respondent, not task.

briefs.title: Randomized sharer profiles for trust and closeness
briefs.question: Does a randomly assigned sharer's trustworthiness or closeness change willingness to share a headline?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Fixes the design cause: randomizing trust and tie removes confounding with real contact traits, and an opt-out answers U1.
briefs.design_sketch: Respondents see single posts, each attributed to a vignette sharer whose relationship (close or distant) and described trustworthiness (low, mid, high) are randomized in a factorial design crossed with information type (true, misinformation, fact-check). The outcome is a 0-100 sharing likelihood plus a 'would not share' option. Quota-sampled US adults answer 8 tasks each, and standard errors are clustered by respondent and task. A subsample also gives a behavioural share-to-feed click.

power_target.basis: Observed close-tie 0.030 and trust-high 0.057; H2 MDE 0.0258 at n 6709/5256, so about 1,500 per cell clustered detects 0.03.

briefs.title: Absolute versus relative misinformation sharing by belief
briefs.question: Do respondents who believe more disputed claims share more misinformation in absolute terms, or only relatively against true content?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Fixes the measurement cause: single-item rating with an opt-out breaks the forced-choice link and answers U2.
briefs.design_sketch: Randomize format between paired forced choice (replication) and independent single-headline sharing with a 'share nothing' option. Information type is randomized within respondent, and belief in disputed claims is measured pre-treatment. Compare the belief by information-type slope across formats. If the slope for misinformation survives in single-item format, the effect is absolute.

power_target.basis: S3 differences of 0.055 to 0.056 with SE 0.017; the interaction across formats needs about double the cell size.

briefs.title: Fact-check effect by topic
briefs.question: Does the fact-check sharing penalty hold for health claims as it does for political claims?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Fixes the sample cause: randomizing topic with adequate health items answers U3.
briefs.design_sketch: Cross information type (true, misinformation, fact-check) with randomized topic (health, political) over a balanced item bank of at least 20 items per topic. Outcome is sharing choice with an opt-out. Sample US adults with oversampled Spanish-language respondents, given the S5 language differences.
briefs.moderator_or_condition: Topic (health versus political), and survey language as a secondary condition

power_target.basis: E2 health fact-check -0.028 (SE 0.028) versus political -0.151; difference of about 0.12 is detectable, but 0.04 targets a smaller health effect; MDE 0.031 at n~4,000 per arm.

verdict: No genuine debate is visible in the retrieved works, which are off-topic (COVID, AI, behavioural policy), so the debates list is empty and the theoretical-debate brief is built on the editor's open question U2 rather than the literature. A follow-up is worth running because the one robust result, the information-type penalty, is already settled, while the interesting claims about trust, closeness and belief-driven sharing rest on measured traits or a forced-choice artefact. Run the randomized-sharer brief first: it resolves U1, the largest threat to the study's contribution, and it is cheap to field within a single wave. The format and topic experiments can follow..
